content: Grapefruit interacts with various medications by inhibiting the hepatic and intestinal enzyme CYP3A4, which is responsible for metabolizing many drugs. This interaction can lead to increased drug levels in the bloodstream, potentially causing enhanced effects or adverse reactions. Below are the detailed effects of grapefruit on specific medications: 1. Neratinib: Grapefruit increases neratinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid coadministration with strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors. Use an alternative drug or monitor closely. 2. Netupitant/Palonosetron: Grapefruit increases levels of netupitant, which is primarily metabolized by CYP3A4. No dosage adjustment is required, but caution and close monitoring are advised. 3. Nicardipine: Grapefruit increases nicardipine levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 4. Nifedipine: Grapefruit doubles the area under the curve (AUC) and maximum concentration (Cmax) of nifedipine without altering its half-life. Avoid grapefruit and grapefruit juice while taking nifedipine. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 5. Nilotinib: Grapefruit increases nilotinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 6. Nimodipine: Grapefruit increases nimodipine levels, but the clinical significance is unknown. Monitor closely. 7. Nintedanib: Grapefruit increases nintedanib levels by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Modify therapy and monitor closely. If adverse effects occur, consider dose reduction, therapy interruption, or discontinuation. 8. Nirogacestat: Grapefruit increases nirogacestat levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. Monitor closely. 9. Nisoldipine: Grapefruit increases nisoldipine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 10. Nitrendipine: Grapefruit increases nitrendipine levels, but the clinical significance is unknown. Monitor closely. 11. Norgestrel: Grapefruit increases norgestrel levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Strong or moderate CYP3A4 inhibitors may increase systemic concentrations of norgestrel, raising the risk of adverse effects. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. 12. Olaparib: Grapefruit increases olaparib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. If coadministration with strong CYP3A inhibitors is unavoidable, reduce the olaparib dose to 150 mg (capsule) or 100 mg (tablet) twice daily. Do not substitute tablets with capsules. 13. Omaveloxolone: Grapefruit increases omaveloxolone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. 14. Ondansetron: Grapefruit increases ondansetron levels, but the clinical significance is unknown. Monitor closely. 15. Osilodrostat: Grapefruit increases osilodrostat levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. 16. Osimertinib: Grapefruit increases osimertinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. If no alternative treatment exists, monitor the patient closely for adverse effects. 17. Oxybutynin: Grapefruit increases oxybutynin levels, but the clinical significance is unknown. Monitor closely. 18. Oxycodone: Grapefruit increases oxycodone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. 19. Paclitaxel: Grapefruit increases paclitaxel levels, but the clinical significance is unknown. Monitor closely. 20. Pacritinib: Grapefruit increases pacritinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction is contraindicated. 21. Palbociclib: Grapefruit increases palbociclib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. If coadministration with strong CYP3A inhibitors is unavoidable, reduce the palbociclib dose to 75 mg/day. 22. Palovarotene: Grapefruit increases palovarotene levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. 23. Panobinostat: Grapefruit increases panobinostat levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction is contraindicated. Strong CYP3A4 inducers can reduce panobinostat levels by approximately 70%, leading to treatment failure. 24. Parecoxib: Grapefruit increases parecoxib levels, but the clinical significance is unknown. Monitor closely. 25. Pazopanib: Grapefruit increases pazopanib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. If coadministration is unavoidable, decrease the pazopanib dose to 400 mg/day. 26. Pexidartinib: Grapefruit increases pexidartinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. 27. Phenytoin: Grapefruit juice has no effect on the pharmacokinetics of phenytoin. 28. Pimavanserin: Grapefruit increases pimavanserin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. If coadministered with strong CYP3A inhibitors, decrease the pimavanserin dose to 17 mg/day. 29. Pimozide: Grapefruit increases pimozide levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction is contraindicated. 30. Pioglitazone: Grapefruit increases pioglitazone levels, but the clinical significance is unknown. Monitor closely. 31. Pirtobrutinib: Grapefruit increases pirtobrutinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. If coadministration is unavoidable, reduce the pirtobrutinib dose by 50 mg. If the current dose is 50 mg/day, discontinue pirtobrutinib for the duration of strong CYP3A inhibitor use. Resume the previous dose after discontinuing the strong inhibitor for five half-lives. 32. Polatuzumab Vedotin: Grapefruit increases polatuzumab vedotin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. Polatuzumab undergoes catabolism to small peptides, amino acids, and monomethyl auristatin E (MMAE), which is a CYP3A4 substrate. Coadministration with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors may increase MMAE levels, leading to toxicity. 33. Pomalidomide: Grapefruit increases pomalidomide levels by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. 34. Ponatinib: Grapefruit increases ponatinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. If coadministration with strong CYP3A inhibitors is unavoidable, reduce the starting dose to 30 mg/day. 35. Pralsetinib: Grapefruit increases pralsetinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. If coadministration is unavoidable, reduce the dose as per prescribing information. Resume the previous dose after discontinuing the strong inhibitor for five half-lives. 36. Praziquantel: Grapefruit increases praziquantel levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 37. Prednisolone: Grapefruit increases prednisolone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 38. Prednisone: Grapefruit increases prednisone levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 39. Primaquine: Grapefruit increases primaquine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. Monitor closely. 40. Propafenone: Grapefruit increases propafenone levels by enhancing gastrointestinal absorption and inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. This applies only to the oral form of both agents. Monitor closely. 41. Quazepam: Grapefruit increases quazepam levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 42. Quetiapine: Grapefruit increases quetiapine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 43. Quinidine: Grapefruit increases quinidine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 44. Quinine: Grapefruit increases quinine levels, but the clinical significance is unknown. Monitor closely. 45. Quizartinib: Grapefruit increases quizartinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Modify therapy and monitor closely. Reduce the dose when coadministered with strong CYP3A inhibitors. Resume the previous dose after discontinuing the strong inhibitor for five half-lives. 46. Rabeprazole: Grapefruit increases rabeprazole levels, but the clinical significance is unknown. Monitor closely. 47. Ramelteon: Grapefruit increases ramelteon levels, but the clinical significance is unknown. Monitor closely. 48. Ranolazine: Grapefruit increases ranolazine levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. Monitor closely. 49. Red Yeast Rice: Grapefruit increases red yeast rice levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. This may increase creatine kinase levels and the risk of myopathy or rhabdomyolysis. Red yeast rice contains monacolin K, which is identical to lovastatin. This interaction is contraindicated. 50. Regorafenib: Grapefruit increases regorafenib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. This interaction is contraindicated. Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors increase regorafenib levels and decrease exposure to its active metabolites (M-2 and M-5). 51. Repaglinide: Grapefruit increases repaglinide levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 52. Repotrectinib: Grapefruit increases repotrectinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. 53. Ribociclib: Grapefruit increases ribociclib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. If coadministration with strong CYP3A inhibitors is unavoidable, reduce the ribociclib starting dose to 400 mg/day. Avoid pomegranates and pomegranate juice as well. 54. Rifaximin: Grapefruit increases rifaximin levels by inhibiting the P-glycoprotein (MDR1) efflux transporter. Use caution and monitor closely. 55. Rimegepant: Grapefruit increases rimegepant levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. 56. Riociguat: Grapefruit increases riociguat levels by decreasing metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. Monitor for signs of hypotension and reduce the dose if needed. 57. Ripretinib: Grapefruit increases ripretinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. Coadministration with strong CYP3A inhibitors increases systemic exposure to ripretinib and its active metabolite (DP-5439), raising the risk of adverse reactions. 58. Ritonavir: Grapefruit increases ritonavir levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 59. Rivaroxaban: Grapefruit increases rivaroxaban levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 60. Romidepsin: Grapefruit increases romidepsin levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 61. Ruxolitinib: Grapefruit increases ruxolitinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. Reduce the starting dose to 10 mg twice daily if platelet count is ≥100 x 10^9/L and a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor is used concurrently. Avoid use if platelet counts are <100 x 10^9/L. 62. Ruxolitinib (Topical): Grapefruit increases topical ruxolitinib levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid grapefruit or use an alternative drug. Reduce the starting dose to 10 mg twice daily if platelet count is ≥100 x 10^9/L and a strong CYP3A4 inhibitor is used concurrently. Avoid use if platelet counts are <100 x 10^9/L. 63. Saxagliptin: Grapefruit increases saxagliptin levels, but the clinical significance is unknown. Monitor closely. 64. Seladelpar: Grapefruit increases seladelpar levels by inhibiting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. This list highlights the importance of avoiding grapefruit or closely monitoring patients when coadministering these medications.
